	 The Supreme Court held that Section 498A is not

marriage.

on disability and digital literacy.

infrastructure;  Livelihood infrastructure;  Climate

Union Minister for Finance and Corporate Affairs, 
Smt. Nirmala Sitharaman, tabled the Union Budget 
2026-27 in the Parliament on February 01, 2026. 
The highlights of  the budget are as follows: 
  Core Theme: 3 Kartavyas
 The Budget targets faster and more resilient growth 
by raising productivity and competitiveness amid 
global volatility.
 The Budget aims to build people’s capacities  so 
citizens become partners in prosperity.
 The Budget seeks inclusive access to resources and 
opportunities for every region and section under 
Sabka Saath, Sabka Vikas. 
  Macro & Fiscal Snapshot (BE 2026–27) 
 Non-debt receipts  are estimated at `36.5 lakh 
crore, and total expenditure is estimated at `53.5 
lakh crore.
 Centre’s net tax receipts  are estimated at `28.7 
lakh crore.
 Gross market borrowings  are estimated at `17.2 
lakh crore, and net borrowings (dated securities) 
are estimated at `11.7 lakh crore.
 Fiscal deficit is estimated at 4.3% of  GDP, while 
RE 2025–26 keeps fiscal deficit at 4.4% of  GDP.
 Debt-to-GDP is estimated at 55.6% (BE 2026–27) 
versus 56.1% (RE 2025–26).
PART-A: Interventions
  Kartavya 1: Growth Push (6 Interventions)
(1) Scale manufacturing in 7 strategic/frontier 
sectors
 The Budget launches Biopharma SHAKTI  with 
`10,000 crore (5 years)  to build India as a global 
biopharma hub.
 The Budget expands biopharma capacity via 3 new 
NIPERs, upgrading 7 NIPERs , and 1,000+ 
accredited clinical trial sites.
 The Budget announces India Semiconductor 
Mission 2.0 for equipment/materials, full-stack IP , 
and supply-chain strengthening with industry-led 
R&D and training.
 The Budget raises Electronics Components 
Manufacturing Scheme outlay to `40,000 crore.
 The Budget proposes Rare Earth Corridors  in 
Odisha, Kerala, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu  
for activities ranging from mining to manufacturing.
 The Budget supports 3 Chemical Parks  through 
a challenge-mode, cluster-based plug-and-play 
model.
 The Budget strengthens capital goods manufacturing 
through Hi-Tech Tool Rooms, CIE equipment 
scheme, and a Container Manufacturing scheme 
with `10,000+ crore (5 years).
 The Budget announces an Integrated Textile 
Programme, including the National Fibre 
Scheme, cluster modernisation, challenge-mode 
Mega Textile Parks, and Mahatma Gandhi Gram 
Swaraj for khadi/handloom/handicrafts.
(2) Rejuvenate legacy industrial sectors
 The Budget announces a scheme to revive 200 
legacy industrial clusters  through tech and 
infrastructure upgrades.
(3) Create “Champion SMEs”
 The Budget introduces an SME Growth Fund of  
`10,000 crore to build future champion firms.
 The Budget tops up the Self-Reliant India Fund 
by `2,000 crore for micro-enterprise risk capital.
 The Budget proposes training ‘Corporate Mitras’  
through professional institutes to provide support in 
Tier-II/III areas.
(4) Infrastructure push
 Public capex is raised to `12.2 lakh crore  in FY 
2026–27.
 An Infrastructure Risk Guarantee Fund  is 
proposed to improve private developer confidence.
 CPSE real-estate recycling is proposed through 
dedicated REITs.
 A new Dedicated Freight Corridor  is proposed 
from Dankuni to Surat.
 20 new National Waterways  are to be 
operationalised in 5 years, starting with NW-5 
(Odisha).
 Regional training centres and ship repair 
ecosystems at Varanasi and Patna are proposed.
 A Coastal Cargo Promotion Scheme  targets 
raising waterways/coastal shipping share from 6% 
to 12% by 2047.
 A Seaplane VGF Scheme is proposed for tourism 
and remote connectivity.
(5) Energy security
 `20,000 crore (5 years) is allocated for Carbon 
Capture, Utilization, and Storage (CCUS) 
technologies.
(6) City Economic Regions (CERs)
 `5,000 crore per CER (5 years)  is announced 
through challenge-mode, reform-cum-results based 
financing.
 Seven High-Speed Rail corridors  are proposed: 
Mumbai–Pune, Pune–Hyderabad, Hyderabad–
Bengaluru, Hyderabad–Chennai, Chennai–
Bengaluru, Delhi–Varanasi and Varanasi–Siliguri.

  Kartavya 3: Sabka Saath, Sabka Vikas 
(Targeted Areas)
 The budget aims to enhance farmer’s through 500

Beverage services.

mental health institutes in Ranchi and Tezpur are 
to be upgraded.

Industrial Corridor, 5 tourism destinations, 4,000 
e-buses, and a Buddhist Circuit Scheme  in NE 
states.

grants for states in FY 2026–27 (as per 16th FC). 
PART –B : Overall Fiscal Framework 
 The Union Government is estimated to spend 
`53.47 lakh crore in 2026–27, representing a 7.7% 
increase over the Revised Estimates (RE) of  2025–
26.
 Interest payments constitute about 26% of  total 
expenditure and absorb nearly 40% of  revenue 
receipts, highlighting persistent debt-servicing 
pressures.
 Total receipts (excluding borrowings)  are 
estimated at `36.51 lakh crore , marking a 7.2% 
increase over the RE of  2025–26, with tax revenue 
expected to grow by 8%.
 The government has projected nominal 
GDP growth at 10%  for 2026–27, reflecting 
expectations of  sustained real growth and moderate 
inflation. 
  De昀椀cit and Debt Targets
 The revenue deficit  is targeted at 1.5% of  
GDP, unchanged from the revised estimate of  
2025–26, indicating continued emphasis on fiscal 
consolidation.
 The fiscal deficit  is targeted at 4.3% of  GDP , 
marginally lower than 4.4% of  GDP in 2025–26 
(RE).
 The Centre has reiterated its commitment to 
reducing outstanding liabilities to around 50% 
of  GDP by March 2031 , with liabilities estimated 
at 55.6% of  GDP in 2026–27.
  Taxation Proposals
 Income tax slabs remain unchanged  for 
Assessment Year 2026–27, maintaining stability in 
the personal tax regime.
 A tax holiday until 2047  has been granted to 
foreign companies providing global cloud 
services using Indian data centres , subject to 
routing services to Indian customers through Indian 
resellers.
 The tax holiday for IFSC units and Offshore 
Banking Units has been extended from 10 years 
to 20 years, with income taxed at 15% thereafter.
 All share buybacks  are proposed to be taxed as 
capital gains , with an additional buyback tax on 
promoters, raising the effective tax rate to 22% for 
corporate promoters and 30% for non-corporate 
promoters.

7% in FY 2025–26 and expects growth to stay near

 It highlights a paradox in which India’s best macro 
performance in decades comes amid a global system 
that no longer reliably rewards discipline with 
currency stability, capital inflows, or insulation.
 The Survey argues that India’s scale population of  
145 crore, and democracy make it unrealistic to copy 
external development templates in a geopolitically 
uncertain world.
 It states that global headwinds can become tailwinds 
if  the State, private sector, and households align 
and sustain a national effort.
 The Survey outlines three global scenarios for 
2026: managed disorder, disorderly multipolar 
breakdown, and a low-probability, high-impact 
shock cascade worse that of  2008.
 Across scenarios, it says India is relatively better 
placed due to a large domestic market, a less 
financialised growth model, strong reserves, and 
credible strategic autonomy, though insulation is not 
complete.
 It warns of  a common risk of  disrupted capital 
flows and sustained rupee pressure that could last 
beyond one year.
 The Survey says India must strengthen foreign 
currency earnings  through exports and investor 
confidence to finance a rising import bill with rising 
incomes.
 It recommends supply stability, strategic buffers, 
diversified trade routes, and alternative payment 
systems, calling for strategic sobriety over defensive 
pessimism.
 It stresses that India must balance long-term growth 
with short-term shock absorption, captured in its 
“marathon and sprint” framing.
 The Survey emphasises process reforms alongside 
policy reforms because administrative processes 
shape citizen-state interaction and reform outcomes.
 It notes that recent deregulation and smart 
regulation by States show the State can shift from 
controller to enabler of  growth.
 It links State capacity, society, and deregulation 
as key pillars for Viksit Bharat and greater global 
influence.
 It urges the State to upskill and mentally prepare 
for a harsher global environment where rules are 
changing.
 It concludes that long-term success requires 
resilience, innovation, and delayed gratification 
rather than quick fixes.
 The Survey has been reorganised into 17 chapters 
based on depth and time-relevance, making it 
broader and longer than earlier editions.
 It includes special essays on AI, quality of  life in 
Indian cities , and how State capacity  and the 
private sector  can build strategic resilience and 
indispensability.
  Key Highlights of  Economic Survey 2025–26
  State of  the Economy
 The global economic environment  remains 
fragile, with elevated risks from geopolitical 
tensions, trade fragmentation , and financial 
vulnerabilities, and some shocks may appear with a 
time lag.
 The First Advance Estimates  project real GDP 
growth at 7.4% and GVA growth at 7.3% for FY26, 
sustaining India’s position as the fastest-growing 
major economy for the fourth consecutive year.
 Potential growth  for India is assessed at around 
7%, while FY27 real GDP growth  is projected at 
6.8%–7.2%.
 Private Final Consumption Expenditure  rises 
by 7.0% in FY26 and reaches 61.5% of  GDP , 
the highest share since 2012 (also seen in FY23), 
supported by low inflation , stable employment, 
and rising real purchasing power.
 Gross Fixed Capital Formation  grows by 7.8% 
in FY26, with investment’s share steady at about 
30% of  GDP, aided by sustained public capex and 
revival in private investment signals.
 The services sector  remains the main growth 
engine, with services GVA rising 9.3% in H1 FY26 
and estimated at 9.1% for the full year. 
  Fiscal Developments
 The Survey states that credible fiscal consolidation 
has reinforced macro-fiscal confidence and is linked 
with three sovereign credit rating upgrades in 2025 
by Morningstar DBRS, S&P Global Ratings, and 
R&I.
 The Centre’s revenue receipts strengthen to 9.2% 
of  GDP in FY25 (PA) , up from an average of  
about 8.5% of  GDP during FY16–FY20.
 Non-corporate tax collections have risen 
structurally, from about 2.4% of  GDP in the 
pre-pandemic period to around 3.3% in the post-
pandemic period.
 The direct tax base  expands, with income tax 
returns filed  increasing from 6.9 crore (FY22)  to 
9.2 crore (FY25), reflecting higher compliance and 
technology-enabled administration.
 Gross GST collections  during April–December 
2025 stand at `17.4 lakh crore, recording 6.7% YoY 
growth, while e-way bill volumes grow 21% YoY 
in the same period, indicating robust transactions.

capacity to spend on social sectors, infrastructure 
and welfare schemes.

 For 2026–27, Bihar’s net budget expenditure  is 
estimated at `3,47,589.76 crore, which is `30,694.74 
crore higher  than the Budget Estimate of 
`3,16,895.02 crore for 2025–26. 
 The annual scheme outlay is `1,22,155.42 crore ,

`2,25,434.34 crore.

expenditure and establishment/committed 
expenditure forms 64.86%.
